prompt.context: Our client is called Blue Chips. They run a silicon manufacturing business, specifically making the quartz that goes into wafers. They are thinking about expanding into the wafer manufacturing business. Wafers come in two diameter sizes – 6 inches and 8 inches. It would cost our client about $200M to expand their factory. Demand in the industry is expected to grow.
prompt.question: Should Blue Chips get into the wafer business? If so, what size of wafer should they produce?

clarifying_info.q: What is the current revenue or profitability of Blue Chips?
clarifying_info.a: Not provided; focus on the expansion decision.

clarifying_info.q: What is the timeline for this expansion?
clarifying_info.a: Not specified; assume near-term strategic decision.

clarifying_info.q: Does Blue Chips have any existing wafer manufacturing capabilities?
clarifying_info.a: No; they currently only make the quartz that goes into wafers.

exhibits.title: Wafer Market Size by Geography
exhibits.shows: A 100% stacked bar chart comparing the geographic revenue breakdown of the 6-inch wafer market and the 8-inch wafer market, with segments for North America, South America, Asia, Europe, and Others. Dollar labels are shown on the North America segments.

framework: Industry Landscape: market size, competitive dynamics, profitability by segment
Investment Analysis: upfront $200M capex, expected payback period
Revenue Potential: achievable market share and revenue by wafer size
Cost Structure: manufacturing costs, process selection (Cz vs Ky)
Market Entry Strategy: how to win share and differentiate

questions.prompt: Calculate the total market size for 6-inch and 8-inch wafers using the exhibit.
questions.guidance: Candidate should read the North America segment dollar value and use the percentage share of North America in each bar to back into the total market size. North America is $300M for 6-inch; if North America represents ~20% of that market, total = $300M / 0.20 = $1.5B. For 8-inch, North America is $420M; if ~25% share, total = $420M / 0.25 = $1.68B. Combined market = $3.18B, round to $3.2B.

math.setup: Read North America dollar values from exhibit, divide by North America's percentage share of each bar to get total market size.
steps: 6-inch: North America = $300M, North America share ≈ 20% → Total = $300M / 0.20 = $1.5B
8-inch: North America = $420M, North America share ≈ 25% → Total = $420M / 0.25 = $1.68B

questions.prompt: Assess the competitive landscape for each wafer size using the revenue data provided by the interviewer.
questions.guidance: For 6-inch: top 3 competitors hold $700M + $350M + $220M = $1.27B out of $1.5B total = ~85% concentration. Market is mostly captured but fragmented below the top 3. For 8-inch: one player holds $1.4B out of $1.68B = ~83% concentration — effectively a near-monopoly. Candidate should note the 8-inch market is more dangerous to enter due to the dominant incumbent, while 6-inch is concentrated but more fragmented below the top.

math.setup: Sum top competitor revenues and divide by total market size.
steps: 8-inch top 1: $1,400M / $1,680M = 83.3% ≈ 83% held by a single player
math.answer: 6-inch: top 3 hold ~85% (more fragmented below). 8-inch: one player holds ~83% (near-monopoly).

questions.prompt: Evaluate profitability: 6-inch wafers have a 7% margin and 8-inch wafers have a 15% margin. How does this change your view?
questions.guidance: Despite the 8-inch market being near-monopolized, its margins are more than double those of 6-inch. Candidate should weigh: 8-inch offers higher profitability per dollar of revenue but faces a very strong incumbent; 6-inch has lower margins but a more accessible competitive structure. A strong candidate will quantify implied profit pools: 6-inch profit pool = $1.5B × 7% = $105M; 8-inch profit pool = $1.68B × 15% = $252M. The 8-inch profit pool is larger but largely captured by the incumbent.

math.setup: Multiply total market size by margin to estimate industry-wide profit pool.
math.answer: 8-inch profit pool ($252M) is 2.4x larger than 6-inch ($105M), but mostly owned by one incumbent.

questions.prompt: How can Blue Chips maximize market share upon entry? Brainstorm ideas.
questions.guidance: This is an open brainstorm; no calculation needed. Candidate should cover multiple levers across product, pricing, go-to-market, and capability-building.

questions.prompt: There are two manufacturing processes: Cz (Czochralski) and Ky (Kyropoulos). For 6-inch Cz: high yield, 20+ year track record, 5 other manufacturers. For 8-inch Cz: very high yield, 2 manufacturers, complex high-tech burning process. For 6-inch Ky: low yield, many competitors. For 8-inch Ky: low yield, similar to 6-inch Ky, no high-tech burning, 2 manufacturers. Which process should Blue Chips use?
questions.guidance: Regardless of wafer size chosen, the Cz process is superior due to higher yield. For 6-inch Cz, the mature process and track record reduce execution risk. For 8-inch Cz, the high yield is attractive but the complex process requires capability investment. Candidate should identify Cz as the preferred process for both sizes and probe cost differences (interviewer can say there are none). The key differentiator is yield, which drives revenue and capacity utilization.

brainstorming.prompt: How can Blue Chips maximize market share when entering the wafer business?

categories.name: Pricing & Commercial
ideas: Penetration pricing to undercut incumbents and win initial customers
Volume discounts to lock in large buyers
Bundled pricing with existing quartz supply (vertical integration advantage)

categories.name: Product & Quality
ideas: Leverage upstream quartz expertise for superior raw material quality
Focus on yield improvement as a differentiator
Offer custom wafer specs for niche applications

categories.name: Customer Acquisition
ideas: Target smaller, underserved customers ignored by dominant players
Partner with semiconductor design houses for co-development
Pursue long-term supply agreements to guarantee volume

categories.name: Operational
ideas: Start with the less capital-intensive size to build capability
Invest in talent and process know-how for Cz manufacturing
Establish quality certifications early to qualify with major OEMs

categories.name: Strategic Positioning
ideas: Position as a vertically integrated supplier (quartz + wafers) for reliability
Emphasize supply chain security in a volatile chip supply environment
Consider joint ventures or licensing to accelerate capability building

recommendation: Blue Chips should enter the wafer manufacturing business, leveraging its existing quartz expertise as a vertical integration advantage.

For wafer size, 6-inch is the more accessible entry point given a less concentrated competitive structure, despite lower margins; however, if Blue Chips can develop Cz process capability, targeting 8-inch could yield higher returns long-term.
The Cz manufacturing process should be adopted for either size due to its superior yield and competitive differentiation.
risks: 8-inch market is near-monopolized; the incumbent may respond aggressively with price cuts or supply lock-ins.
$200M capex is significant; payback depends on achieving meaningful market share in a concentrated market.
Cz process for 8-inch is technically complex; execution risk is high without existing process expertise.
Demand growth assumption must hold; if semiconductor demand softens, the investment case weakens.
next_steps: Conduct detailed customer interviews to assess willingness to switch suppliers and identify underserved segments.
Model IRR and payback period under different market share scenarios (e.g., 5%, 10%, 15% share).
Assess internal Cz process capability gaps and estimate cost to build vs. acquire know-how.
Evaluate whether to enter 6-inch first as a stepping stone before scaling to 8-inch.
